answer: Organic solutes (mainly sucrose) are actively loaded into sieve tubes at the **source** (e.g., leaves), raising osmotic pressure and drawing in water. This creates high turgor pressure. answer: Xerophytes are plants adapted to arid (dry) environments. Adaptations include: (1) thick waxy cuticles to reduce cuticular transpiration, (2) sunken stomata in pits to trap humid air, and (3) leaves reduced to spines (e.g., cacti) to minimise surface area for water loss.

answer: Halophytes are plants that grow in saline (salty) soils (e.g., mangroves). They actively transport excess salts into their vacuoles (salt sequestration), making the cell's water potential more negative than the surrounding soil, so water enters by osmosis.

answer: Mesophytes open their stomata when water is plentiful to promote transpiration and gas exchange, and close them during water scarcity (via ABA signalling) to prevent desiccation. They are adapted to moderate, well-watered habitats.

answer: Turgor pressure is the hydrostatic pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall, generated when water enters the central vacuole by osmosis.
